Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) -- Two of the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr.'s children are suing their brother, accusing him of wrongfully taking money from their parents' estates. Dexter King, left, Bernice King and Martin Luther King III attend a 2006 tribute for their late mother. Bernice King and Martin Luther King III allege that Dexter King took "substantial funds" out of Coretta Scott King's estate and "wrongfully appropriated" money from their father's estate. The suit, filed Thursday in Fulton County Superior Court, serves as a very public fissure in an iconic family that has always professed unity, particularly as questions have swirled around some of their financial dealings. In a written statement Friday, Dexter King called the suit "inappropriate and false." "I'm disappointed that our personal family disagreement, as it relates to the family business, has evolved into being handled in a public legal forum," he said. "It is my hope that this inappropriate and false claim by my siblings will be swiftly resolved and we can go about the business of focusing on our parents' tremendous legacy." The Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in April 1968 in Memphis, Tennessee, where he was to lead garbage workers on a protest march. King's wife, Coretta Scott King, also devoted her life to the civil rights movement, died in 2006. Attorneys for Bernice King and Martin Luther King III would not say Friday how much money they are accusing Dexter King of taking from their mother's estate. Bernice King is the administrator of that estate. Dexter King, the suit says, controls their father's estate, which is registered as a Georgia corporation. All three children are shareholders in that corporation. The lawsuit names Dexter King and the corporation as defendants. It alleges that last month, the defendants "converted substantial funds from the estate's financial account at Bank of America for their own use." Harmon Caldwell, an Atlanta attorney representing the plaintiffs, said Dexter King is a signatory on the account, but "was not authorized to transfer the funds," and gave his sister "no notice that those funds were being transferred." The suit says that as a result of the transfer, "plaintiffs have and will suffer financial loss." The lawsuit lists Bernice King as a plaintiff both individually and as administrator of their mother's estate. Separately, the suit says Dexter King "has wrongfully appropriated assets belonging to the [estate of the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr.] or its shareholders for his own benefit." Caldwell said Dexter King has refused to say what has happened with some of the corporation's money. "I can't tell you that he's gone out and used corporate assets for his own living expenses," the attorney said. "What I can tell you for certainty is that by not providing Martin and Bernice with information about how the corporation is using its assets, he is essentially using those assets, appropriating those assets for his own benefit." The plaintiffs' attorneys would not estimate the size of either estate. But one, Jock Smith, noted that a collection of King's manuscripts and other items was sold in 2006 for a reported $32 million. "I don't think it was a substantial corporation of any sort before that," Smith said. Over the years, the family of the civil rights leader has zealously protected its financial interests, at times taking legal steps even against the media for showing some of King's most famous speeches. In 2005, some news agencies reported on the King Center, a nonprofit, having put millions of dollars into a for-profit business run by Dexter King. The family rejected allegations of wrongdoing, and has generally pushed to keep financial matters private. Smith said his clients made repeated efforts to reach out to their brother in recent weeks before deciding to take legal action. Smith agreed with the suggestion that it was emotionally tough for the King children to file the suit. "That would be the understatement of the year, Smith said.

ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) — A dispute over the estates of the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King has led two of their children to take their brother to court.

Bernice King and Martin Luther King III filed a lawsuit Thursday in Fulton County Superior Court against Dexter King and the Georgia corporation that holds their father’s estate. They claim Dexter removed a significant amount of money from their mother’s estate and improperly used assets connected to their father’s estate for his own benefit.

All three siblings—pictured together at a 2006 memorial honoring their late mother, with Dexter on the left—are shareholders in the corporation. Dexter controls their father’s estate, while Bernice serves as administrator of their mother’s estate.

The legal action publicly exposes a rift within a famous family known for presenting a united front, even as scrutiny has arisen over some of its financial activities.

Dexter denied the accusations in a statement issued Friday, describing them as both false and unsuitable. He said he regretted that a private disagreement involving the family business had moved into a public courtroom. He also expressed hope that the matter would be resolved quickly so the siblings could return their attention to preserving their parents’ extraordinary legacy.

Martin Luther King Jr. was killed in Memphis, Tennessee, in April 1968. He had traveled there to lead sanitation workers in a protest march. His wife, Coretta Scott King, dedicated her life to the civil rights cause as well and died in 2006.

Lawyers representing Bernice and Martin declined Friday to disclose the amount they believe Dexter took from their mother’s estate. According to the complaint, Dexter and the corporation transferred a large sum from the estate’s Bank of America account last month and used it for their own purposes.

Harmon Caldwell, an Atlanta lawyer for the plaintiffs, said Dexter was authorized to sign on the account but did not have permission to move the money. Caldwell added that Bernice received no advance warning about the transfer. The complaint maintains that the transaction has caused, and will continue to cause, financial harm to the plaintiffs.

Bernice is named as a plaintiff both personally and in her role as administrator of Coretta Scott King’s estate.

The lawsuit separately accuses Dexter of improperly taking property belonging either to Martin Luther King Jr.’s estate or to the corporation’s shareholders for his personal advantage. Caldwell said Dexter has declined to explain what became of some corporate funds.

The attorney said he could not claim that Dexter had directly spent corporate money on personal living costs. However, Caldwell argued that Dexter’s refusal to tell Bernice and Martin how the corporation’s assets were being handled effectively amounted to using and controlling those resources for his own benefit.

The plaintiffs’ legal team would not provide an estimate of the value of either parent’s estate. One of their attorneys, Jock Smith, pointed out that a collection of King’s papers and other materials reportedly sold for $32 million in 2006. Smith said he did not believe the corporation had been particularly substantial before that sale.

King’s family has long guarded its economic interests closely. At times, relatives have pursued legal action against media organizations for broadcasting some of the civil rights leader’s best-known speeches.

In 2005, several news outlets reported that the nonprofit King Center had invested millions of dollars in a for-profit company operated by Dexter. The family denied that anything improper had occurred and has generally sought to keep its financial affairs out of public view.

Smith said Bernice and Martin repeatedly attempted to contact their brother during the weeks before they chose to sue. Asked whether bringing the case had been emotionally difficult for the King children, Smith replied that describing it that way “would be the understatement of the year.”

# King family dispute spills into court over civil rights leader’s estate

**ATLANTA** — A long-running disagreement among the children of the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. became a public legal battle after two of the civil rights leader’s children accused their brother Dexter King of mishandling family estates and using assets for his own benefit.

Martin Luther King III and the Rev. Bernice King alleged in court filings that Dexter, who oversaw the business affairs connected to their father’s estate, failed to provide adequate financial records and improperly exercised control over valuable family property. The complaint also raised questions about the proceeds from the reported $32 million sale of King’s collection of manuscripts, speeches and other historical documents.

Dexter denied the accusations. Through his attorney, he characterized the claims as false and said his actions had been taken in accordance with his responsibilities to the estate and its beneficiaries.

The dispute placed three of King and Coretta Scott King’s four children on opposing sides of a case involving both family finances and stewardship of one of the most important private archives in American history. Their eldest daughter, Yolanda King, died in 2007.

## Allegations of withheld records and personal use of assets

In their lawsuit, Martin III and Bernice alleged that Dexter had exercised broad control over Estate of Martin Luther King Jr. Inc., the entity that manages the civil rights leader’s intellectual property, licensing rights and other assets.

They accused him of refusing or failing to provide complete information about the estate’s finances and transactions. The filings also alleged that he had converted or diverted estate property for personal use, although the precise value of the assets at issue was not publicly established.

The allegations were civil claims and had not been proven in court.

The plaintiffs sought a full accounting and judicial oversight of the estate’s affairs. They also questioned Dexter’s handling of their mother’s estate, arguing that his role created concerns about conflicts of interest and whether all beneficiaries were being treated fairly.

Coretta Scott King died in January 2006. Her estate plan generally contemplated that her children would share in her property, while the family’s interests in their father’s intellectual property continued to be administered through a separate corporate structure. Dexter held important management and fiduciary positions in those arrangements, giving him significant authority over records, royalties and transactions.

That structure had long required the siblings to operate not only as family members but also as business partners — a combination that intensified disagreements over control and disclosure.

## Questions surrounding the $32 million archive transaction

A central point of contention involved the 2006 acquisition of Martin Luther King Jr.’s papers for a reported $32 million.

The collection — including handwritten drafts, correspondence, sermons, notes and other documents — had been offered for sale and was at one point headed for auction. Atlanta civic leaders intervened, assembling private funding to keep the archive in King’s hometown. The papers were acquired and placed at Morehouse College, King’s alma mater, where they could be preserved and made available for scholarship.

Martin III and Bernice’s lawsuit did not challenge the historic importance of keeping the papers in Atlanta. Instead, it sought information about how the transaction was handled, how the money was received and distributed, and whether all beneficiaries were given a complete accounting.

The archive sale was especially sensitive because the papers carried both substantial financial value and enormous symbolic importance. Control of the documents meant influence over how King’s legacy would be preserved, licensed and presented to the public.

## Dexter King rejects the claims

Dexter responded that the lawsuit contained inaccurate and damaging allegations. His legal team maintained that he had not misappropriated estate assets and that he had acted properly in managing the family’s business interests.

Attorney Jock Smith, representing Dexter, disputed the siblings’ account and described the allegations as unfounded. Smith said Dexter would defend his stewardship and rejected the suggestion that he had used his position to enrich himself improperly.

Dexter’s response also reflected a broader divide within the family over how the King legacy should be managed. He had long taken an active role in protecting the commercial use of his father’s name, image and writings — a strategy supporters viewed as necessary to prevent exploitation, but critics sometimes regarded as overly restrictive or opaque.

## Attorneys describe a family conflict that reached a breaking point

Harmon Caldwell, an attorney for Martin III and Bernice, said the pair had turned to the courts only after efforts to obtain information privately failed. Caldwell portrayed the lawsuit as a last resort aimed at securing transparency, rather than an attempt to damage Dexter personally.

He said his clients wanted a detailed accounting of estate assets and transactions and believed court intervention was necessary to protect their interests.

Smith, Dexter’s attorney, countered that the accusations unfairly impugned his client’s character and management. He said Dexter denied wrongdoing and would answer the claims through the legal process.

The sharply different statements underscored how far the family relationship had deteriorated. What began as an internal disagreement over records, authority and estate administration had become a public fight over money, trust and control of the King name.

The case also highlighted the unusual burdens faced by the heirs of major historical figures. The King siblings inherited not only family property but also responsibility for speeches, manuscripts, photographs, licensing rights and an international legacy closely tied to the civil rights movement.

For the court, however, the immediate questions were narrower: whether Dexter fulfilled his legal duties, whether he provided the disclosures required of him, and whether estate assets and proceeds — including those connected to the multimillion-dollar manuscript sale — were properly handled.

Those questions were left to be resolved through evidence and judicial review, as one of America’s most prominent families confronted its divisions in public.
